title: 22. Interview: NGINX
summary: Interview Q&A for NGINX — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 NGINX interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is NGINX's event-driven architecture able to handle 10K+ concurrent connections where Apache's prefork model struggles?
**Answer:** Apache prefork uses one process per connection, so 10,000 concurrent connections require 10,000 processes. Each process has its own address space, stacks, and interpreter state — typically 2-8 MB of RSS per process, so 10K connections means 20-80 GB of RAM just for connection state, plus the OS overhead of context-switching between 10K processes on each I/O. NGINX inverts this: a small number of worker processes (one per CPU core), each running a single-threaded event loop using `epoll` (Linux) or `kqueue` (BSD). Each worker can manage 10K+ connections via non-blocking sockets — when a connection is waiting on I/O, the worker doesn't block; it registers the FD with `epoll` and moves to the next ready connection, returning only when the kernel signals data is ready. The memory cost per idle connection is just a few KB (the connection struct and read/write buffers), so 10K connections on one worker is ~50 MB, not 50 GB. The trade-off: NGINX workers must never block on synchronous I/O, so any third-party module that does blocking I/O (e.g., a sync database call) stalls the entire worker — this is why NGINX module development requires careful async discipline or Lua/OpenResty.
**Visual:**
```
Apache prefork (1 process per conn):   NGINX (1 worker per CPU, epoll):
  10K conns = 10K processes = 60GB RAM   4 workers x 10K conns each = 40K conns
  context-switch overhead per I/O        memory: ~50MB/worker, no switching
  MAX ~1-2K concurrent per box           MAX ~50K+ concurrent per box
```

### Q2. What is the difference between NGINX's `http` block (Layer 7) and `stream` block (Layer 4)?
**Answer:** The `http` block does Layer 7 load balancing: NGINX parses HTTP requests (method, URL, headers, body), can route based on URL path (`location /api/`), manipulate headers, terminate SSL, serve cached responses, and so on. Backends see a normal HTTP request — NGINX adds `X-Forwarded-For`, `Host`, etc. The `stream` block does Layer 4: NGINX proxies raw TCP/UDP bytes without parsing the application protocol. It's used for non-HTTP protocols — PostgreSQL on port 5432, Redis on 6379, MySQL on 3306, or proprietary binary protocols. The `stream` block can still load-balance (round-robin, least_conn) across multiple backends and do SSL termination for TLS-wrapped protocols, but it can't route by URL or HTTP header. The choice depends on the protocol: HTTP traffic goes in `http` for the rich features; everything else goes in `stream`. A typical config uses `http` for the public-facing web tier and `stream` for an internal database proxy (e.g., to load-balance reads across PostgreSQL replicas or to terminate SSL for an internal service that doesn't natively support TLS).
**Visual:**
```
http {                    stream {
  server {                  server {
    listen 443;               listen 5432;
    location /api/ {          proxy_pass pg_replicas;
      proxy_pass api;       }
    }                       }
  }                       }
}                        }
L7: parse HTTP, route     L4: raw TCP bytes, no parsing
   by URL/header             just by destination port
```

### Q3. How does NGINX terminate SSL and why is this useful?
**Answer:** SSL termination means NGINX handles the TLS handshake with the client (presents the certificate, decrypts incoming bytes, encrypts outgoing responses) and proxies the decrypted request to the backend over plain HTTP (or re-encrypted HTTPS via `proxy_pass https://...`). This is useful for four reasons. (1) **CPU offload** — TLS encryption is computationally expensive (AES-GCM at 10 Gbps needs dedicated CPU); centralizing it at NGINX (which can use hardware acceleration, OpenSSL async, or even specialized TLS cards) lets application servers focus on business logic. (2) **Certificate centralization** — instead of installing and rotating certificates on every backend, you install them only on NGINX; one cert update is one place. (3) **HTTP-level features** — once decrypted, NGINX can route by URL path, rewrite headers, inject `X-Forwarded-*`, do path-based load balancing, and serve cached responses — impossible if traffic remains encrypted end-to-end. (4) **SNI multiplexing** — NGINX can serve thousands of certificates on one IP/port via Server Name Indication, choosing the cert based on the `Host` header / SNI in the ClientHello. The trade-off is that traffic between NGINX and the backend is unencrypted (over a private network, this is usually acceptable; over a public network, use `proxy_pass https://...`). End-to-end TLS (mTLS between NGINX and backend) is the secure alternative for sensitive workloads.
**Visual:**
```
client ==TLS==> NGINX (terminate, decrypt) ==HTTP==> backend
                  cert here, backend sees plain HTTP

vs end-to-end:
client ==TLS==> NGINX ==mTLS==> backend (cert here too)
```

### Q4. What is the role of the master process vs the worker processes in NGINX?
**Answer:** The **master process** is the supervisor: it reads and parses `nginx.conf`, binds listening ports (80, 443, etc.), forks the worker processes, and watches them. If a worker dies (crash, OOM), the master restarts it. The master also handles signals: `nginx -s reload` causes the master to re-read config, spawn new workers with the new config, and send `TERM` to old workers (which finish in-flight requests, then exit) — this is the zero-downtime config reload. The **worker processes** do the actual work: each worker enters an event loop, calls `epoll_wait`, accepts connections, parses requests, proxies to upstreams, and writes responses. Workers are single-threaded (one thread per worker) and independent — they don't share state, so each worker maintains its own upstream round-robin counter and connection pool. The number of workers is set by `worker_processes` (typically `auto`, which equals the CPU core count). The master never handles client traffic — it's only the supervisor. This separation is what enables zero-downtime reloads: the master can orchestrate worker replacement while old workers drain, and a worker crash doesn't take down the whole NGINX (the master restarts it).
**Visual:**
```
master (pid 1)         workers (one per CPU core)
  - parse config          - epoll event loop
  - bind ports            - accept connections
  - fork workers          - parse HTTP, proxy_pass
  - reload (SIGUSR2)      - SSL terminate
  - restart crashed       - round-robin upstreams
    workers
```

### Q5. How does NGINX do zero-downtime config reload, and what are the gotchas?
**Answer:** `nginx -s reload` (or `kill -HUP <master_pid>`) triggers a reload. The master receives SIGHUP, re-parses the config, and if valid, forks new worker processes with the new config. It then sends SIGTERM to the old workers — but the old workers don't die immediately; they stop accepting new connections and finish in-flight requests, then exit gracefully (default 60-second timeout, after which they're force-killed). The result is zero client-visible downtime. **Gotchas:** (1) **Long-lived connections** — WebSocket or gRPC streams established before the reload will keep old workers alive until they complete or hit the 60s timeout; a reload under heavy WS load can leave old workers lingering for minutes. (2) **Upstream changes** — adding a backend requires a reload; the new workers see the new pool, but old workers finish their existing connections with the old pool. (3) **Syntax errors** — if `nginx -t` (config test) isn't run first and the new config has a syntax error, the master rejects it and keeps the old workers (no reload happens); if a reload somehow uses a bad config, NGINX may fail to start new workers while old workers continue with the old config. (4) **Frequent reloads** — each reload forks new workers, which re-warms caches, re-establishes upstream connections; reloading every few seconds causes performance dips. For dynamic upstream changes (e.g., Kubernetes pod churn), use `ngx_http_dyups_module` or NGINX Plus's API to add/remove backends without reload.
**Visual:**
```
nginx -s reload:
  master re-parses config (validated)
  master forks NEW workers with new config
  master sends SIGTERM to OLD workers
    OLD: stop accepting new conns, drain in-flight (60s max), exit
    NEW: accept all new conns
  client-visible: nothing (zero downtime)
  gotcha: long-lived WS/gRPC on OLD workers block exit
```

### Q6. What is OpenResty / ngx_lua, and when would you use it instead of plain NGINX config?
**Answer:** OpenResty is a bundle of NGINX + the `ngx_http_lua_module` that lets you embed Lua code directly in `nginx.conf`. The Lua code runs inside the NGINX worker process via LuaJIT (a fast Lua compiler), can access request data (headers, body, cookies, args), make sub-requests to upstreams, manipulate the response, and even run external network calls (Redis, MySQL, HTTP) — all non-blocking via NGINX's cosocket API. Use cases: (1) **programmable edge logic** — rate-limiting by user ID, JWT validation, request rewriting based on database lookups, A/B testing routing; (2) **API gateway** — Kong is built entirely on OpenResty and provides plugin-based API management; (3) **WAF** — Cloudflare's edge WAF runs Lua rules inside NGINX for per-request inspection at line rate. The advantage over plain NGINX config is dynamic logic; the advantage over a separate API gateway (like Envoy) is performance (Lua runs in-process, no IPC). The disadvantage is operational complexity — debugging Lua inside NGINX requires understanding NGINX's request phases (`rewrite`, `access`, `content`, `log`, etc.), and a bug in Lua code can crash the entire worker. For most teams, plain NGINX for SSL/routing plus a separate API gateway for business logic is simpler; OpenResty is for teams that need the performance of in-process edge logic.
**Visual:**
```
plain NGINX:                 OpenResty (NGINX + Lua):
  location /api/ {             location /api/ {
    proxy_pass api;              access_by_lua_block {
  }                                if not validate_jwt() then
                                     return 401
                                   end
                                   local rs = redis:get("rate:"..client_ip)
                                   if tonumber(rs) > 100 then return 429 end
                                 end
                                 proxy_pass api;
                               }
  (static routing)              (programmable, in-process, line rate)
```

### Q7. When would you choose NGINX over HAProxy or Envoy?
**Answer:** **NGINX** is the swiss army knife — web server, reverse proxy, L4/L7 LB, SSL termination, caching, HTTP/2/3 — in one binary with the most mature ecosystem and documentation. Choose NGINX when you need multiple roles at the edge (serve static files + proxy dynamic + terminate SSL + HTTP/2) and want one tool. **HAProxy** is more focused — purely a high-performance L4/L7 load balancer with the best stats page, sophisticated algorithms (slow-start, dynamic weight), and a reputation for bulletproof reliability under high throughput. Choose HAProxy when the sole job is load balancing (e.g., in front of a database, or as a dedicated L4 LB for TCP traffic) and you need fine-grained algorithm control. **Envoy** (from Lyft/CNCF) is the modern successor — dynamic configuration via xDS APIs (no reloads to change upstreams), deep observability (per-request tracing built-in), and first-class service-mesh integration (Istio, Consul). Choose Envoy for cloud-native dynamic environments (Kubernetes, service mesh) where backends change every minute and reloads are unacceptable. Real-world: Netflix uses NGINX at the edge (SSL, HTTP routing) and Zuul for app logic; Instagram uses NGINX + OpenResty heavily; Stack Overflow and Reddit famously use HAProxy; Lyft, Square, and many K8s-native shops use Envoy.
**Visual:**
```
NGINX:    edge needs (SSL, HTTP/2, static files, proxy) -> one tool
HAProxy:  pure L4/L7 LB for high-throughput, fine-grained algorithms
Envoy:    cloud-native, dynamic config, service mesh, deep observability
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your NGINX-served API occasionally returns 502 Bad Gateway under high load. How do you debug?
**Answer:** 502 means NGINX couldn't get a valid response from the upstream. Debug step by step. (1) Check NGINX `error.log` for the specific upstream failure — common messages: "upstream timed out", "upstream prematurely closed connection", "no live upstreams". (2) If "upstream timed out": the backend is too slow — increase `proxy_read_timeout` (default 60s) or fix the backend. (3) If "upstream prematurely closed connection": the backend closed the connection mid-response — often a backend crash (OOM, segfault) or a keep-alive mismatch (NGINX sends a keep-alived request to a backend that just closed the connection). (4) If "no live upstreams": NGINX marked all backends as down via passive health checks — check the backend pool. (5) Under high load specifically: the backend may be queueing requests and hitting `proxy_connect_timeout` (default 60s) because the listen queue (somaxconn / `proxy_backlog`) is full. Fixes: increase `worker_connections` (default 512/1024 — set to 10240 for high load), `keepalive_requests`, and `keepalive_timeout` to reduce connection churn; ensure backends have enough capacity; tune `proxy_connect_timeout` and `proxy_read_timeout` to realistic values; enable `proxy_next_upstream` to retry on a different backend on 502/timeout. Also check `ulimit -n` (file descriptor limit) — NGINX with 10K connections needs 20K+ FDs.
**Visual:**
```
502 under load -> check error.log:
  "upstream timed out"      -> backend too slow / proxy_read_timeout too low
  "no live upstreams"       -> all backends marked down, fix backend health
  "prematurely closed"     -> backend crash or keep-alive mismatch
fix: worker_connections 10240, keepalive, proxy_next_upstream, ulimit -n
```

### Q2. You need to dynamically add/remove backend servers in NGINX without reloading. How?
**Answer:** Open-source NGINX requires a config reload (`nginx -s reload`) to change the upstream pool — the upstream server list is compiled at config parse time and is immutable at runtime. Reloads are zero-downtime but cause a brief performance dip (new workers re-warm caches, re-establish upstream connections). Three options for dynamic upstreams. (1) **NGINX Plus** (commercial) — exposes a REST API (`PATCH /upstreams/{name}/servers/{id}`) to add/remove servers live with no reload. (2) **Third-party module `ngx_http_dyups_module`** — adds a similar dynamic-upstream API to open-source NGINX; not in the default build but compileable. (3) **DNS-based upstreams** — use `server api.example.com:8080 resolve;` in the upstream block; NGINX periodically re-resolves the DNS name (per the DNS TTL) and updates the pool automatically. This works well with Kubernetes Services (which are DNS names) — as pods are added/removed, the Service's DNS reflects the new endpoints, and NGINX picks them up on the next re-resolution. The trade-off: DNS-based has a delay (DNS TTL, often 5-30s in K8s) and requires the `resolver` directive to specify a DNS server. For most K8s deployments, the **Ingress controller pattern** (NGINX Ingress Controller, which watches the K8s API and triggers reloads on Endpoint changes) is the standard — reloads happen, but the controller batches them to avoid reload storms.
**Visual:**
```
options:
  NGINX Plus REST API     -> live, no reload (paid)
  ngx_http_dyups_module   -> live, compile-in (open-source)
  DNS-based upstreams     -> periodic re-resolve, delay = DNS TTL
  Ingress controller      -> watches K8s API, reloads on endpoint change
```

### Q3. You're serving a single domain with NGINX but need to route `/api/*` to one backend pool and `/static/*` to a CDN. How do you configure it?
**Answer:** Use `location` blocks within a single `server` block. The `server` block matches the `Host` header (your domain); the `location` blocks match URL prefixes. `/api/` proxies to the API backend pool; `/static/` either proxies to a CDN origin or (better) redirects to the CDN URL so the client fetches directly from the CDN edge. Sample config:

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name example.com;
    ssl_certificate /etc/nginx/cert.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/key.pem;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://api_backend;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }

    location /static/ {
        return 301 https://cdn.example.com$request_uri;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://web_backend;
    }
}
```

The `proxy_set_header` directives are critical: without them, the backend sees NGINX's IP, not the client's. `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends to any existing `X-Forwarded-For` chain. The `301` redirect for `/static/` means the client fetches static assets directly from the CDN, offloading that traffic entirely from your NGINX.
**Visual:**
```
example.com/api/users   -> proxy_pass http://api_backend (pool of API servers)
example.com/static/x.js -> 301 redirect to cdn.example.com/static/x.js
example.com/            -> proxy_pass http://web_backend (SSR or frontend)
```

### Q4. Your NGINX workers are hitting 100% CPU under high load. How do you diagnose and tune?
**Answer:** 100% CPU on NGINX workers usually means the event loop is busy doing CPU-bound work, not just I/O. Diagnose: (1) `top -H -p <nginx_pid>` to see per-thread CPU — if one worker is saturated, it's a hot loop in that worker. (2) Check `nginx -V` to confirm you have the right modules enabled (some debug modules add overhead). (3) Use `strace -p <worker_pid> -c` to see which syscalls dominate — `epoll_wait` should be most common; if `read`/`write` dominate, the worker is doing too much I/O; if `crypt` or AES syscalls dominate, you're SSL-bound. (4) Use `perf top -p <worker_pid>` to see which functions burn CPU. Common causes and fixes: **SSL-bound** — enable TLS 1.3 (faster handshake), use AES-NI (modern CPUs have hardware AES), offload SSL to a separate NGINX tier with TLS accel cards; **regex-bound** — `location ~ \.php$` regex compiled per-request? Use simple prefixes (`location /api/`) where possible; **Lua-bound** — `access_by_lua` running heavy logic per request? Cache results in `ngx.shared.dict`; **insufficient workers** — `worker_processes auto` should match CPU cores; if only 1 worker on a 16-core box, you're wasting 15 cores; **connection churn** — disable keep-alive between client and NGINX? Enable `keepalive_timeout 65; keepalive_requests 100;`. Finally, ensure `worker_rlimit_nofile` is high enough (typically 100K+) and `worker_connections` is set to 10240+.
**Visual:**
```
top -H: worker pid 1234 = 100% CPU
  strace -c: epoll_wait 60%, read 30%, write 10% (I/O healthy)
  perf top: SSL_write 70% -> SSL-bound!
fix: TLS 1.3, AES-NI, separate SSL tier, cert session reuse
```

### Q5. You want to enable HTTP/2 on NGINX. What changes, and what are the pitfalls?
**Answer:** Enabling HTTP/2 is one line: change `listen 443 ssl;` to `listen 443 ssl http2;` in each `server` block. HTTP/2 requires TLS in practice (browsers don't support h2c over plain TCP), so it goes hand-in-hand with SSL termination. Pitfalls: (1) **HTTP/2 push is deprecated** — `http2_push` was removed from most browsers in 2022; don't rely on it. (2) **Coalescing** — if multiple subdomains (e.g., `api.example.com` and `www.example.com`) resolve to the same IP and use the same cert (SAN cert), browsers will reuse one HTTP/2 connection for both, which can break `Host`-based routing in surprising ways. (3) **Worker connections** — HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection, so `worker_connections` matters less but the per-connection buffer usage is higher; tune `http2_body_preread_size`. (4) **Head-of-line blocking** — HTTP/2 still has TCP-level HoL blocking; HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes this, but requires the `nginx-quic` build (mainline since 1.25.0). (5) **Mixed HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1** — backends typically speak HTTP/1.1 (or you need `proxy_http_version 1.1`), so NGINX speaks HTTP/2 to the client and HTTP/1.1 to the backend; this is fine but means HTTP/2 features like multiplexing don't extend to the backend (that would require gRPC or HTTP/2-to-HTTP/2 proxying). Test with `curl --http2 -I https://example.com` and verify the response header.
**Visual:**
```
listen 443 ssl http2;  <-- single directive enables HTTP/2

client <-HTTP/2 multiplex-> NGINX <-HTTP/1.1 keep-alive-> backend
       (one TCP, many reqs)        (separate TCP per backend)
```

### Q6. Your NGINX Ingress Controller in Kubernetes is reloading every few seconds due to pod churn. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** Each pod add/remove triggers a config change, which the Ingress Controller translates to an NGINX reload — at high pod churn (e.g., during a deployment, HPA scaling, or many microservices), this can mean reloads every few seconds, causing performance dips and connection churn. Fixes: (1) **Enable dynamic upstream configuration** — the NGINX Ingress Controller has a `--enable-dynamic-configuration` flag (default in recent versions) that uses Lua to update upstreams without reload for endpoint changes (only reload for Ingress rule changes, not pod IP changes). (2) **Batch reloads** — the controller can coalesce multiple endpoint changes into a single reload with a small delay (e.g., 1 second). (3) **Use a different Ingress controller** — Envoy-based controllers (Contour, Gloo, Emissary) don't reload at all; they update Envoy's config via xDS API dynamically. (4) **Stable upstreams** — if you use headless Services and `proxy_pass http://api.example.com resolve;`, NGINX re-resolves periodically (DNS TTL) and picks up new pod IPs without a reload. (5) **Reduce pod churn** — if HPA is scaling too aggressively (every minute), tune the HPA thresholds and stabilization window to reduce churn. The production pattern is: NGINX Ingress Controller with dynamic configuration enabled, headless Services with reasonable DNS TTLs, and reduced churn via HPA tuning. For very dynamic environments, consider Envoy-based ingress.
**Visual:**
```
problem: pod churn -> endpoint change -> reload -> perf dip (every few sec)
fixes:
  --enable-dynamic-configuration   (Lua updates upstreams, no reload)
  headless Service + resolve       (NGINX re-resolves DNS, no reload)
  batch reloads with delay         (coalesce multiple changes)
  switch to Envoy-based ingress    (no reloads ever)
```

### Q7. You're migrating from Apache to NGINX. What configuration differences and gotchas should you expect?
**Answer:** Several. (1) **No `.htaccess`** — Apache processes per-directory `.htaccess` files on every request, which is a performance hit but allows per-app config without root. NGINX reads only the central `nginx.conf`, so .htaccess-style rules must be moved into `location` blocks in the main config and require a reload to change. (2) **No `mod_rewrite` RewriteRule** — NGINX uses `rewrite` directive (similar but different syntax) and `try_files` for the common "if file doesn't exist, send to index.php" pattern. (3) **No `mod_php`** — Apache runs PHP in-process via `mod_php`; NGINX requires PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager) as a separate process, with `fastcgi_pass 127.0.0.1:9000;`. This is actually faster (PHP-FPM has its own process management) but requires setup. (4) **Path-based routing syntax** — Apache uses `<Location>`, NGINX uses `location`. (5) **SSL config differences** — Apache uses `SSLEngine on; SSLCertificateFile`, NGINX uses `listen 443 ssl; ssl_certificate`. (6) **Reverse proxy syntax** — Apache uses `ProxyPass /api/ http://backend/`, NGINX uses `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://backend; }`. (7) **No built-in `.htpasswd`** — NGINX supports `auth_basic` with `htpasswd` files (same format as Apache), but you generate the file with `htpasswd` from Apache tools or `openssl passwd`. The migration is mostly mechanical but requires careful testing, especially for rewrite rules — Apache's rewrite engine is more featureful, and complex rules may need rethinking in NGINX.
**Visual:**
```
Apache:                              NGINX:
  <VirtualHost *:80>                   server {
    ServerName example.com              listen 80;
    ProxyPass /api/ http://b/          server_name example.com;
    <Directory /var/www>                 location /api/ { proxy_pass http://b; }
      AllowOverride All                 location / {
    </Directory>                          root /var/www;
  </VirtualHost>                          index index.php;
                                        }
                                      }
  .htaccess per-dir                   (no .htaccess, central config only)
  mod_php in-process                  PHP-FPM via fastcgi_pass
```

options: 100% CPU on NGINX workers usually means the event loop is busy doing CPU-bound work, not just I/O.
NGINX is the swiss army knife — web server, reverse proxy, L4/L7 LB, SSL termination, caching, HTTP/2/3 — in one binary with the most mature ecosystem and documentation.
Open-source NGINX requires a config reload (nginx -s reload) to change the upstream pool — the upstream server list is compiled at config parse time and is immutable at…
nginx -s reload (or kill -HUP ) triggers a reload. The master receives SIGHUP, re-parses the config, and if valid, forks new worker processes with the new config.
quiz.explanation: nginx -s reload (or kill -HUP ) triggers a reload. The master receives SIGHUP, re-parses the config, and if valid, forks new worker processes with the new config. It then sends SIGTERM to the old workers — but the old workers don't die immediately; they stop accepting new connections and finish in-flight requests, then exit gracefully (default 60-second timeout, after which they're force-killed).
